scenes.title: SELF JOIN
scenes.narration: A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using aliases, letting you relate rows within the same table.

scenes.title: Why join a table to itself
bullets: Model hierarchies like employee and manager.
Compare one row against another in the same table.
Requires two aliases to tell the copies apart.
scenes.narration: Self joins let you model hierarchies such as an employee pointing to their manager within one table. They also let you compare rows against each other, for example to find pairs or sequences. Because both sides are the same table, you must give it two aliases so the query can distinguish the copies.

scenes.title: How to build a self join
steps: List the table twice with different aliases.
Pick the column that links a row to another row.
Write the ON clause between the two aliases.
Select columns from each alias as needed.
scenes.narration: You start by listing the same table twice under two distinct aliases. Then you identify the column that connects one row to another, such as a manager_id pointing at an id, and write the ON clause between the aliases. From there you select the columns you need from each side.

scenes.title: Employees and their managers
scenes.code:
SELECT e.name AS employee,
       m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
INNER JOIN employees AS m
  ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
scenes.narration: Here the employees table is joined to itself, with alias e for the worker and alias m for the manager. The ON clause links each employee's manager_id to the employee_id of another row, which is the manager. Selecting from both aliases gives us the employee's name next to their manager's name.

scenes.title: Include top-level staff with LEFT JOIN
scenes.code:
SELECT e.name AS employee,
       m.name AS manager
FROM employees AS e
LEFT JOIN employees AS m
  ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
scenes.narration: The inner-join version drops anyone without a manager, such as the CEO. Switching to a left join keeps every employee, and shows NULL as the manager for people at the top of the hierarchy. This ensures the whole org chart is represented rather than only the middle layers.

scenes.title: Self join vs ordinary join

left.title: Self join
points: Both sides are the same table.
Relates rows to other rows in one table.

scenes.narration: A self join and an ordinary join use the same syntax; the only real difference is that a self join names one table on both sides. Because the names would otherwise collide, aliases become mandatory. Conceptually you are relating rows to other rows in the same set.

scenes.text: Self joins are the natural fit for parent-child hierarchies and for comparing rows within a single table.
scenes.narration: Reach for a self join whenever you have a parent-child hierarchy or need to compare rows inside a single table.
